summary.text: Encoding each reversed row as pairs \([x,1]\) reduces its evolution to a binary run derivative; endpoint identities for three iterates give a seven-dimensional positive recurrence for the associated lengths, whose positive weighted mass is multiplied by the number \(r>1\) satisfying \(r^4(r-1)^3=1\). This yields two-sided constant multiples of \(r^n\) for the binary-word lengths, and the row-sum increment formula together with the row-length lower bound transfers those estimates to the row sums, so squeezing their \(n\)-th roots gives the limit \(r\).

full_proof.text:
Let \(T_n\) denote the rows of A381587, indexed as in the question, and put
\[
S_n=\sum_{x\in T_n}x.
\]
Thus \(S_n=A381358(n)\). For a finite word \(u\), let \(R(u)\) be its list of run lengths. The defining recurrence is
\[
T_1=[1],\qquad T_2=[1],\qquad T_3=[2],
\]
and, for \(n\geq 4\),
\[
T_n=R(T_{n-1}^{\rm rev})\,T_{n-1},                 \tag{1}
\]
where juxtaposition denotes concatenation and “rev” denotes reversal. We will prove that there is a real number \(r>1\), characterized by
\[
r^4(r-1)^3=1,                                      \tag{2}
\]
such that \(S_n^{1/n}\to r\). (Numerically, \(r\approx1.5550575766\).)

The main issue is to obtain a finite-dimensional recurrence controlling the lengths of the rows. We first develop a binary encoding of their structure.

Define an operation \(D\) on finite binary words (with letters \(0,1\)) as follows. Reading from left to right, every \(0\) emits nothing, while a \(1\) emits \(1\) if its following letter is \(0\), and emits \(0\) if its following letter is \(1\) or if it is the last letter. Equivalently,
\[
D(\varnothing)=\varnothing,
\]
\[
D(0u)=D(u),
\]
and
\[
D(1u)=\begin{cases}
1D(u),&u\text{ begins with }0,\\
0D(u),&u\text{ begins with }1\text{ or }u=\varnothing.
\end{cases}
\]
Let
\[
H(u)=D(u)^{\rm rev}.
\]
Starting with \(W_0=[1]\), define binary words recursively by
\[
W_{n+1}=W_nH(W_n).                                  \tag{3}
\]

We record the word identities that will be needed. They all follow directly by reading the definition of \(D\). For arbitrary binary words \(u,v\),
\[
D(u1v)=D(u)D(1v),
\]
and hence
\[
H(u1v)=H(1v)H(u).                                   \tag{4}
\]
In particular, if the displayed \(1\) is the last letter of \(u1\) and is followed by a \(0\), then the letter it emits changes from \(0\) to \(1\). Thus
\[
H((u1)0v)=H(v)1H(u).                                \tag{5}
\]

For completeness, another useful way to organize the boundary calculation is via the “gap-indicator” word \(G(u)\), defined recursively by
\[
G(\varnothing)=[0],\qquad G(1u)=0G(u),
\]
\[
G(0u)=1\,\operatorname{tail}(G(u)).
\]
An induction on \(u\) gives
\[
D(1u)=G(u).                                         \tag{6}
\]
The same induction, separating the last letter, gives
\[
G(u1)=G(u)0,
\]
\[
G(u0)=\operatorname{dropLast}(G(u))1,
\]
and consequently
\[
G(u^{\rm rev})=G(u)^{\rm rev}.                     \tag{7}
\]
Combining (6) and (7), one obtains the boundary-shift identity
\[
H((v1)^{\rm rev})0=D(1v1).                          \tag{8}
\]
This identity is what closes the induction below at the right endpoint of a word.

The first few consequences of (3) are also immediate. For every \(n\geq0\),
\[
W_{n+1}=10v\quad\text{for some word }v,             \tag{9}
\]
because \(W_1=10\) and every later word has its predecessor as a prefix. Moreover, for every \(n\geq0\),
\[
W_{n+2}=1(v1)\quad\text{for some word }v.           \tag{10}
\]
Indeed, write \(W_{n+1}=10v\). By (4) and the definition of \(H\), one has \(H(10v)=H(v)1\), so
\[
W_{n+2}=10vH(v)1.
\]
In particular, every \(W_m\) with \(m\geq2\) ends in \(1\).

We next prove the key delayed third-derivative identity. For every \(n\geq0\),
\[
H(W_{n+6})=00v_n,                                   \tag{11}
\]
\[
H^2(W_{n+6})=00u_n,                                 \tag{12}
\]
for suitable words \(v_n,u_n\), and
\[
H^3(W_{n+6})=\operatorname{tail}(W_{n+2})^{\rm rev}.\tag{13}
\]
Here \(H^j\) denotes \(j\)-fold iteration.

We include the induction because (13) is the substantive combinatorial fact in the proof. Direct calculation from (3) gives
\[
W_6=101010110011100010111,
\]
\[
H(W_6)=000110010111,
\]
\[
H^2(W_6)=000110,
\]
\[
H^3(W_6)=10.
\]
Since \(W_2=101\), the last word is indeed \(\operatorname{tail}(W_2)^{\rm rev}=01^{\rm rev}=10\). This proves the base case.

Suppose (11)–(13) hold for a word \(W=W_{n+6}\). By (10), \(W\) ends in \(1\). Two consequences of (4) and (5) will be used. First, whenever \(W\) ends in \(1\) and \(H(W)=0z\),
\[
H(WH(W))=H^2(W)\,1\,\operatorname{tail}(H(W)).      \tag{14}
\]
To see this, write \(W=x1\) and \(H(W)=0z\), and apply (5) to \((x1)0z\). The relation \(H(x)=z\), which follows by comparing \(H(x1)=0z\), gives exactly (14).

Second, if in fact \(H(W)=00z\), applying \(H\) once more to (14), using (4) at the inserted \(1\), gives
\[
H^2(WH(W))=H^2(W)\,1\,H^3(W).                      \tag{15}
\]
Because \(H^2(W)\) begins with \(00\), equations (14) and (15) show that both \(H(W_{n+7})\) and \(H^2(W_{n+7})\) again begin with \(00\). This proves (11) and (12) at the next index.

It remains to update (13). Apply \(H\) to the right side of (15), substitute the inductive identity
\[
H^3(W)=\operatorname{tail}(W_{n+2})^{\rm rev},
\]
and write, using (10), \(W_{n+2}=1(s1)\). Formula (4) moves the distinguished inserted \(1\) through the reversal, and formula (8) accounts for its final emitted bit. The resulting word is
\[
\operatorname{tail}\bigl(W_{n+2}H(W_{n+2})\bigr)^{\rm rev}
 =\operatorname{tail}(W_{n+3})^{\rm rev}.
\]
This is (13) with \(n\) replaced by \(n+1\), and completes the induction.

We now connect this binary process to the actual triangle. For a list \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_k)\) of positive integers, define
\[
P(x)=[x_1,1,x_2,1,\ldots,x_k,1].
\]
Thus
\[
|P(x)|=2|x|.                                        \tag{16}
\]
Define an integer “gap” operation \(Q_k\) recursively by
\[
Q_k(\varnothing)=[k],

t\]
\[
Q_k(xw)=\begin{cases}
Q_{k+2}(w),&x=1,\\
k\,Q_1(w),&x\ne1.
\end{cases}                                         \tag{17}
\]
The entries of \(Q_k(w)\) are the odd lengths of the blocks of \(1\)'s which arise when one scans \(P(w)\), beginning with an already accumulated block of length \(k\).

A direct run decomposition gives the following precise identity. If \(a\ne1\), then
\[
R(P(aw))^{\rm rev}=P(Q_1(w)^{\rm rev}).             \tag{18}
\]
Here is why. A block of \(j+1\) equal symbols followed by a different symbol contributes the run length \(j+1\); a terminal block of \(j+1\) equal symbols contributes the singleton list \([j+1]\). Applying these observations successively to
\[
a,1,x_1,1,x_2,1,\ldots
\]
shows that every occurrence \(x_i=1\) lengthens the current block of \(1\)'s by two, while every \(x_i\ne1\) closes that block, then contributes a run of length one and starts a new block of \(1\)'s of length one. This is exactly recursion (17), and reversing the run list gives (18).

Define integer words \(N_n\) by
\[
N_0=[2],
\]
\[
N_{n+1}=N_n\,Q_1(\operatorname{tail}(N_n))^{\rm rev}.\tag{19}
\]
Every \(N_n\) begins with \(2\). From (18), (19), and the triangle recurrence (1), induction on \(n\) yields
\[
T_{n+4}^{\rm rev}=P(N_n).                           \tag{20}
\]
The base case is \(T_4=[1,2]\), so \(T_4^{\rm rev}=[2,1]=P([2])\). For the induction step, reverse (1): the old reversed row is followed by the reverse of its run-length list. Equation (18) says that this new part is exactly the paired word associated to the second term in (19), proving (20).

Mark an integer by \(1\) if it is different from \(1\), and by \(0\) if it equals \(1\). Under this marking, the integer gap operation becomes the binary derivative. More precisely, for any positive \(k\), marking \(Q_k(w)\) produces a word whose first bit records whether \(k\ne1\), and whose remaining bits are obtained by the derivative rule. This follows immediately by induction in (17): an entry equal to \(1\) changes \(k\) to \(k+2\), which is certainly different from \(1\), while an entry different from \(1\) emits the current marker and restarts with \(k=1\). In the special case needed here,
\[
\operatorname{mark}(Q_1(w))=D(1\operatorname{mark}(w)).\tag{21}
\]
Using the fact that \(N_n\) begins with \(2\), equations (19) and (21) show inductively that
\[
\operatorname{mark}(N_n)=W_n.                      \tag{22}
\]
Taking lengths in (20), and using (16) and (22), gives the crucial row-length formula
\[
|T_{n+4}|=2|W_n|.                                   \tag{23}
\]

For any finite word \(u\), its run lengths sum to its length:
\[
\sum R(u)=|u|.                                      \tag{24}
\]
This is simply because the runs partition the positions of \(u\). Also,
\[
|R(u)|\le |u|,                                      \tag{25}
\]
since every run is nonempty. From (1), (23), and (24),
\[
S_{n+5}=S_{n+4}+2|W_n|.                             \tag{26}
\]
Furthermore,
\[
|T_{n+4}|\le S_{n+4}.                               \tag{27}
\]
One may prove (27) by induction. It is true for \(T_4=[1,2]\). In passing from \(T_m\) to \(T_{m+1}\), the new length is \(|T_m|+|R(T_m^{\rm rev})|\le2|T_m|\) by (25), whereas the new sum is \(S_m+|T_m|\ge2|T_m|\) if \(|T_m|\le S_m\).

We now derive the promised finite-dimensional recurrence. Regard the following lengths as real numbers:
\[
A_n=|W_n|,\qquad B_n=|H(W_n)|,\qquad C_n=|H^2(W_n)|.
\]
Equation (3) gives, for all \(n\),
\[
A_{n+1}=A_n+B_n.                                    \tag{28}
\]
Taking lengths in (14), and using that \(H(W_{n+6})\) begins with \(00\), gives
\[
B_{n+7}=B_{n+6}+C_{n+6}.                            \tag{29}
\]
Indeed, the right side of (14) has length
\(C_{n+6}+1+(B_{n+6}-1)\). Similarly, taking lengths in (15), then using (13) and the fact that \(W_{n+2}\) is nonempty, yields
\[
C_{n+7}=C_{n+6}+A_{n+2}.                            \tag{30}
\]
These are the seven-coordinate positive linear recurrences alluded to in the construction.

We also have the elementary inequalities
\[
0<A_n,
\qquad 0\le B_n\le A_n,
\qquad 0\le C_n\le B_n\le A_n.                    \tag{31}
\]
Indeed, \(W_n\) is nonempty, and \(D\) emits at most one letter for every input letter. Equation (28) also shows that \(A_n\) is nondecreasing.

We next choose the exponential rate. The function
\[
f(x)=x^4(x-1)^3
\]
is continuous on \([1,2]\), with \(f(1)=0\) and \(f(2)=16\). The intermediate value theorem therefore supplies \(r\in[1,2]\) satisfying (2). It cannot equal \(1\), so \(r>1\).

Put \(d=r-1>0\), and define the positive weighted mass
\[
\begin{aligned}
M_n={}&r^3A_{n+2}+r^2A_{n+3}+rA_{n+4}+A_{n+5}\\
&+r^4d^2A_{n+6}+r^4dB_{n+6}+r^4C_{n+6}.             \tag{32}
\end{aligned}
\]
Substitution of (28)–(30) gives the exact identity
\[
M_{n+1}=rM_n.                                       \tag{33}
\]
We spell out the coefficient check. After replacing
\[
A_{n+7}=A_{n+6}+B_{n+6},
\]
\[
B_{n+7}=B_{n+6}+C_{n+6},
\]
\[
C_{n+7}=C_{n+6}+A_{n+2},
\]
the coefficients in \(M_{n+1}\) of \(A_{n+2},A_{n+3},A_{n+4},A_{n+5}\) are respectively \(r^4,r^3,r^2,r\), as in \(rM_n\). The coefficient of \(A_{n+6}\) is
\[
1+r^4d^2=r^5d^2,
\]
because \(1=r^4d^3\). The coefficient of \(B_{n+6}\) is
\[
r^4(d^2+d)=r^4d(d+1)=r^5d,
\]
and that of \(C_{n+6}\) is
\[
r^4(d+1)=r^5.
\]
Thus all coefficients agree. Iterating (33),
\[
M_n=M_0r^n.                                         \tag{34}
\]
All terms in (32) are nonnegative and its first term is positive, so \(M_n>0\).

Define
\[
K=r^3+r^2+r+1+r^4d^2+r^4d+r^4>0,
\qquad \alpha=r^4d^2>0.
\]
By monotonicity of \(A_n\) and (31), every length occurring in (32) is at most \(A_{n+6}\). Therefore
\[
M_n\le K A_{n+6}.                                   \tag{35}
\]
On the other hand, retaining only the \(r^4d^2A_{n+6}\) term gives
\[
\alpha A_{n+6}\le M_n.                             \tag{36}
\]
Combining (34)–(36), we obtain positive constants
\[
c=\frac{M_0}{K},\qquad D=\frac{M_0}{\alpha}
\]
such that, for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
c r^n\le A_{n+6}\le D r^n.                        \tag{37}
\]

It remains to transfer these bounds from word lengths to row sums. By (23) and (27),
\[
2A_{n+6}=|T_{n+10}|\le S_{n+10}.
\]
Together with the lower bound in (37), this implies
\[
c r^n\le S_{n+10}.                                 \tag{38}
\]
For the upper bound, equation (26), shifted by six places, reads
\[
S_{n+11}=S_{n+10}+2A_{n+6}.                         \tag{39}
\]
Choose
\[
U=S_{10}+\frac{2D}{r-1}>0.
\]
Then \(S_{10}\le U\), and
\[
2D\le U(r-1).                                       \tag{40}
\]
We claim inductively that
\[
S_{n+10}\le Ur^n.                                  \tag{41}
\]
The case \(n=0\) is the choice of \(U\). If it holds at \(n\), then by (37), (39), and (40),
\[
S_{n+11}
 \le Ur^n+2Dr^n
 \le Ur^n+U(r-1)r^n
 =Ur^{n+1}.
\]
Thus (41) holds for all \(n\). Combining (38) and (41),
\[
c r^n\le S_{n+10}\le Ur^n                         \tag{42}
\]
with \(c,U>0\).

Take positive real \((n+10)\)-th roots in (42):
\[
(c r^n)^{1/(n+10)}
 \le S_{n+10}^{1/(n+10)}
 \le (U r^n)^{1/(n+10)}.                            \tag{43}
\]
For every fixed \(E>0\),
\[
(E r^n)^{1/(n+10)}
 =E^{1/(n+10)}r^{n/(n+10)}\longrightarrow 1\cdot r=r,

y
\]
because \(1/(n+10)\to0\) and \(n/(n+10)\to1\). Applying this first with \(E=c\) and then with \(E=U\), the squeeze theorem applied to (43) gives
\[
S_{n+10}^{1/(n+10)}\longrightarrow r.
\]
Removing the fixed shift of ten indices does not change convergence at infinity. Consequently
\[
\boxed{\displaystyle \lim_{n\to\infty} A381358(n)^{1/n}=r},
\]
where \(r>1\) satisfies \(r^4(r-1)^3=1\). In particular, the requested limit exists.
